source.filename: 2020-A novel design of SMA based soft robotic gripper with variable stiffness.pdf

constitutive_assumptions: Thermal elasticity coefficient theta of the SMA wire is much smaller than phase transformation coefficient Omega and elastic modulus E, and is ignored.
Initial strain and stress values of the SMA wire are assumed to be 0.
Stress-induced martensite term (epsilon_L * xi_L) is small and neglected, simplifying the SMA constitutive equation.
The variable stiffness joint is assumed to behave as a cantilever beam.
Gravity is neglected in the joint deflection calculation.
The joint is assumed to deform in a circular arc under bending.
Heat loss from the paraffin to the environment is ignored due to encapsulation by the silicone membrane.
Initial phase fractions before transformation are initialized as martensite xi_M = 1 and austenite xi_A = 0.
control_variables: Applied heating voltage to Ni-Cr wire (10 V)
Applied heating voltage to SMA wire (6 V)
Finger dimensions (length 120 mm, width 20 mm, thickness 30 mm)
Joint design parameters (l1 = 20 mm, l2 = 25 mm, assembly distance D = 30 mm, assembly angle theta = 70°)
Force sensor displacement rate and step interval (1 mm increments up to 10 mm)
Diameter of fixed cylinder during vertical pulling test (85 mm)
dependent_variables: Thermal response times (heating time to 58 °C and cooling time to solid state)
Robotic finger stiffness (slope of force vs. displacement)
Finger bending angle and multi-posture configurations
Vertical pulling force during upward motion
Grasping force (net pulling force minus gripper weight)
Holding capability / grasp stability with and without active SMA actuation

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A single robotic finger achieves an approximate 18-fold stiffness variation between the liquid state (0.0136 N/mm) and solid state (0.2431 N/mm) of paraffin.
Variable stiffness joints enhance the gripper's maximum grasping force by approximately 10-fold, increasing from 0.57 N at low stiffness to 5.66 N at high stiffness.
Paraffin heating to its melting point of 58 °C with an embedded Ni-Cr wire takes about 70 s at 10 V, while natural cooling to the solid state takes about 380 s.

Independently modulating the stiffness of two embedded joints per finger combined with SMA wire actuation enables four distinct configurations: straight, joint-1 bending, joint-2 bending, and simultaneous bending.
At high stiffness, the soft gripper can stably hold a 500 g water bottle even after turning off power to the SMA actuator wire.

An analytical framework couples SMA Joule heating, empirical phase transformation kinetics, constitutive stress-strain relationships, and cantilever beam mechanics to relate heating time to joint bending angle.

experimental_setup: Infrared thermometer setup measuring paraffin temperature variation at 10 s intervals during heating (10 V) and natural air cooling.

Fingertip stiffness measurement setup using a DYLY-103 tension-compression force sensor (range 0–50 N, comprehensive error 0.03% FS) driven along a screw linear guide over a 10 mm horizontal displacement (1 mm intervals) with a pre-tensioned pulling cord.
Maximum grasping force test bench where the three-fingered gripper grasps a fixed 85 mm cylinder and moves vertically upward by 42 mm while measuring vertical pulling force.

Multi-object manipulation testing platform demonstrating adaptive grasping on objects of various geometries (a square box, a smooth thin-walled cylinder, an orange, and a 500 g water bottle) under different stiffness and actuation states.
future_work: Optimization and experiments to shorten the transition time required to change stiffness from low stiffness to high stiffness.
independent_variables: Phase/temperature state of paraffin (solid vs. liquid / high vs. low stiffness) via Ni-Cr wire heating voltage and cooling duration
SMA actuation state (applied voltage of 6 V vs. unpowered)
Selective joint activation (joint-1, joint-2, or both joints)
Applied horizontal displacement at the fingertip (0 to 10 mm in 1 mm steps)
Object geometry, surface characteristics, and weight (box, smooth thin cylinder, orange, 500 g water bottle, 85 mm cylinder)
limitations_inferred: Reliance on passive natural cooling results in a slow cycle time (380 s to stiffen), which severely restricts operating speed and dynamic grasping tasks.
Continuous electrical power is required to hold the deformed configuration during the multi-minute cooling phase before the paraffin solidifies.
Heat dissipation through the silicone encapsulation over repeated thermal cycles may affect surrounding structures and repeatable phase transformation temperatures.
The payload capacity (500 g) and maximum grasping force (5.66 N) remain relatively low for heavier robotic manipulation tasks.
Cantilever beam and circular arc assumptions do not capture 3D multi-axial deformations, contact compliance, or viscoelastic effects in the silicone casing.
limitations_stated_by_authors: A long time is required for changing the joint from low stiffness to high stiffness (380 s cooling time), which increases the overall time needed to grasp objects.
main_results: The single robotic finger demonstrated an 18-fold stiffness change, with stiffness measuring 0.2431 N/mm in the solid state and 0.0136 N/mm in the liquid state.
The maximum grasping force of the three-fingered gripper increased by approximately 10 times with variable stiffness joints, reaching 5.66 N at high stiffness compared to 0.57 N at low stiffness.
Heating the paraffin to its 58 °C melting point required approximately 70 s, while natural cooling back to the solid state took approximately 380 s.
Each finger achieved four distinct postures (straight, joint-1 bending, joint-2 bending, simultaneous bending) through selective joint heating and SMA wire contraction.
The soft gripper successfully grasped objects of diverse shapes (square box, cylinder, orange) and stably held a 500 g water bottle at high stiffness without active SMA power.
modeling_methods: Thermal heat transfer model of SMA wire considering Joule heating and convective cooling to ambient air
SMA hysteresis thermal phase transformation model (martensite-to-austenite and austenite-to-martensite kinetics)
Cantilever beam deflection model for the flexible joint under bending moment generated by SMA wire force
Ni-Cr wire electrical Joule heating and paraffin thermal absorption energy balance model
Kinematic model relating SMA wire shrinkage, joint deflection, and circular arc bending angle
Geometric gripping volume model determining minimum and maximum graspable object radii from base angle and finger dimensions
performance_metrics: Finger stiffness at high stiffness (K1 = 0.2431 N/mm) and low stiffness (K2 = 0.0136 N/mm), representing an 18-fold enhancement
Heating time to reach paraffin melting point (70 s) and cooling time to return to solid state (380 s)
Maximum reaction force at 10 mm displacement (2.21 N at high stiffness vs. 0.14 N at low stiffness)
Maximum vertical pulling force (8.73 N at high stiffness vs. 3.28 N at low stiffness)
Maximum grasping force (5.66 N at high stiffness vs. 0.57 N at low stiffness, ~10-fold ratio)
Theoretical object grasping diameter range (21 mm to 90 mm)
Maximum payload demonstrated without continuous SMA power (500 g water bottle)
possible_gap_implications: The long thermal relaxation time (~380 s) indicates that practical implementation of phase-change materials in soft robotics requires active cooling methods or hybrid mechanisms.

Simplifying assumptions in the joint model (ignoring heat dissipation through the elastomer and viscoelastic mechanics) suggest a need for comprehensive multi-physics thermo-mechanical models for encapsulated phase-change soft actuators.

The trade-off between compliance at low stiffness and modest maximum grasping force (5.66 N) highlights the potential for investigating hybrid rigid-soft reinforcement structures to achieve higher payloads.
paper.research_objective: To propose, model, fabricate, and experimentally validate an SMA-based soft robotic gripper with embedded variable stiffness paraffin joints capable of compliant grasping at low stiffness and shape-retentive, high-force holding at high stiffness for manipulating objects of irregular shapes and varied weights.
paper.research_problem: Soft robotic grippers suffer from low grasping forces due to soft actuator properties and an inability to vary stiffness during grasping, which limits their application range and load capacity.
stiffness_mechanism: resistance wire (Ni-Cr) Joule heating and natural cooling
paper.title: A novel design of shape-memory alloy-based soft robotic gripper with variable stiffness
